Hey everyone,

Recently I just started getting back into 40k and am finding that my painting skills are pretty mediocre. Given the pretty high cost of models, I wouldn't mind stripping the paint off some of my models and trying again to improve my painting. I did a bit of research on dakka-dakka and a few other hobby sites to see if there was a way to do so without damaging the models, unfortunately there was very little information on the topic. Any stuff I did find, like using Dettol or motor-oil, was heavily debated with half saying it works while another half saying it turned the models 'squishy'. I was wondering if anyone had any success with stripping paint on finecast models, coz forking out an extra $60 just to replace a terrible looking squad is pretty painful for my bank account.

Thanks in advance!
Paint removal on Citadel Finecast Models

Simple Green. I've used it with plastic, resin (finecast), and metal and it's been safe on each. Fill a small sealed tubberware container or whatnot and let your figures soak for a few hours or overnight for tougher paints (I wouldn't go past that though, it is a solvent afterall), then take a brush to them the next morning. You'll get 99% of the paint off if not all.

I think the Yes Power Spray that /u/andli826 recommended is just a localized version of it, so if you live outside US or Sweden you might have to find your own variant I guess. They should all be more or less the same though.

Also, you can test it on a sprue or something first if you're really worried.
They've changed the formula on Fairy/Yes Powerspray so it no longer works. It, strangely, used to be one of the best ways to strip minis. Even better than denatured alcohol or acetone.

That sounds like they went for a more green formula or something. There might still be a max strength/industrial version on the market for you guys perhaps, unless the active chemical got straight up outlawed or something.

I would be really scarred to bring acetone anywhere near plastic or resin though, it melts plastics so well people often use it to 'weld' plastic pieces together. With a lot of care and some diluting you could probably use it just enough to eat only the paint though. I wonder how good mineral spirits would work..

Retired programmer here. It seems to me the requirements need to be clearly stated (e.g. prevent new user brigading the website (I'm not even sure what that is)), list different options, evaluate how well it does or does not meet the requirements, and then we can discuss a better one. I'm sure that design work has already been done in one form or another but I'm not aware of the results. Anything I bring up has probably already been discussed.
Brigading is when a mass of users from a subverse go to another subverse to specifically upvote/downvote something.

Having the option to sort your feed by "Most Upvotes", "Upvote %" and "Hybrid" (a combination of the two) may not be a bad idea, but ultimately, the content that is popular with the majority is going to be the highest rated in all three of those, and controversial opinions will almost certainly not sneak in to the top page even if downvotes are removed completely.

Social Networks that are focused on people's real names, their friends and their social lives have a good reason to stick with only offering a like option, as has been the case with Facebook from the very beginning. It's disingenuous and incorrect to say, "a lot of companies are going just to upvotes (ie Google and Facebook) for sorting content."

Social News Sites like Fark, Digg, Reddit and Voat are fulfilling a very different role, and just like many forums that have been around for decades, offering users the ability to upvote and downvote comments helps the community. While they're different ways to implement and use downvoting, I definitely don't think removing it would be in Voat's, or it's users, best interest.
